 1                       MEMORANDUM OF POINTS AND AUTHORITIES
 2   I.     INTRODUCTION
 3          This case arises out of Meta Platforms, Inc.’s (“Meta”) policy against “Child Sexual
 4   Exploitation” (“CSE”), whereby Meta prohibits content or activity that sexually exploits or
 5   endangers children. Pro se Plaintiff Marvelle J. “Jay” Ballentine brings this suit against Meta,
 6   Accenture LLP (“Accenture”), TaskUs, Inc. (“TaskUs”) and Genpact Limited (“Genpact”)
 7   (collectively, “Defendants”), alleging that Accenture, TaskUs, and Genpact (collectively, the
 8   “Vendor Defendants”) are all vendors that review appeals from users challenging CSE (or other)
 9   policy violations on Meta’s services. Plaintiff brings this suit against all Defendants because Meta
10   allegedly disabled Plaintiff’s Facebook account pursuant to Meta’s CSE policy, and one of its
11   vendors—he has no idea which—allegedly affirmed the disablement. Based solely on his
12   allegations that a Vendor Defendant had access to information showing that Plaintiff is Black when
13   it upheld the disablement and that, in a handful of other CSE enforcement cases (out of millions),
14   Meta allegedly reversed the initial determinations for white users, Plaintiff summarily accuses
15   Defendants of disabling his account based on his race and asserts a claim under 42 U.S.C. § 1981
16   (“Section 1981”).
17          Plaintiff’s Second Amended Complaint (“SAC”) is the latest in a long series of complaints
18   stemming from the alleged disablement of his Facebook account that Plaintiff has filed against
19   some combination of the Defendants (and, remarkably, their counsel) across several courts. And,
20   although Defendants have filed motions to dismiss each of Plaintiff’s prior complaints, including
21   motions to dismiss the same Section 1981 claim he asserts in the SAC, Plaintiff’s litigation strategy
22   of amending his complaints or voluntarily dismissing actions before Defendants’ motions to
23   dismiss are decided has prevented a ruling on the merits of Defendants’ arguments for dismissal.
24   Plaintiff’s present Section 1981 claim fails for the same reasons as his prior Section 1981 claims
25   and should be dismissed, with prejudice, for several reasons.
26          First, despite Plaintiff’s attempts to plead around it, Plaintiff’s claim against each Defendant
27   is barred by Section 230(c)(1) of the Communications Decency Act (“Section 230”), which bars
28   claims against interactive computer service providers and users based on the removal of content,

                                                                   DEFS’ MOT. TO DISMISS SECOND AM. COMPL.
                                                       1                              NO. 3:26-CV-5939-RFL

Case 3:26-cv-05939-RFL          Document 152           Filed 08/13/26     Page 10 of 25



 1   including user accounts, from their services. Plaintiff cannot circumvent that bar by bringing suit
 2   against Meta’s vendors for content-moderation services or conspicuously replacing his prior
 3   allegations regarding the disablement of his Facebook account with vague allegations that
 4   Defendants interrupted his ability to perform third-party contracts.
 5           Second, Plaintiff’s claim under 42 U.S.C. § 1981 is insufficiently pled because Plaintiff fails
 6   to plead any facts showing that any Defendant engaged in intentional racial discrimination.
 7   Moreover, Plaintiff’s Section 1981 claim against the Vendor Defendants fails for the independent
 8   reason that Plaintiff engages in improper group pleading, alleging that one of the Vendor
 9   Defendants affirmed his account disablement, without specifying which Vendor Defendant (if any)
10   actually acted here.
11   II.     BACKGROUND
12           Procedural History:1 Plaintiff filed his original complaint against Meta and Accenture in
13   this district on September 9, 2025, asserting claims under several federal civil rights statutes
14   (including 42 U.S.C. § 1981) based on allegations that Meta disabled Plaintiff’s Facebook account
15   and Accenture affirmed the disablement because of Plaintiff’s race. See Marvelle J. “Jay”
16   Ballentine v. Meta Platforms, Inc., et al., No. 3:25-cv-7671-CRB (N.D. Cal.). After Meta and
17   Accenture moved to dismiss Plaintiff’s complaint, and the court declined to allow him discovery
18   pending resolution of the motions to dismiss and shortly before argument was scheduled on the
19   motions, Plaintiff voluntarily dismissed this first action and re-filed his claims in the Middle District
20   of Florida. See Dkt. No. 1.
21           In the Middle District of Florida, Plaintiff raised substantially similar claims as those raised
22   in his original Northern District of California action, based on essentially identical factual
23   allegations, but added Genpact and TaskUs as additional defendants. Id. In particular, Plaintiff
24   alleged that he is a “Black business owner” who “operated [a] mobile RV repair business” and used
25   Facebook for advertising purposes until Meta allegedly disabled his Facebook account on July 4,
26   1
      A full summary of Plaintiff’s nearly year-long history of pursuing litigation against the Defendants
27   across several different courts, including Plaintiff’s practice of continuously filing amended
     complaints in response to motions to dismiss, voluntarily dismissing his complaints before
28   resolution of the motions to dismiss, and seeking early discovery before any ruling on motions to
     dismiss, is contained in Defendants’ Joint Status Report. See Dkt No. 148.
                                                                     DEFS’ MOT. TO DISMISS SECOND AM. COMPL.
                                                        2                               NO. 3:26-CV-5939-RFL

Case 3:26-cv-05939-RFL          Document 152           Filed 08/13/26     Page 11 of 25



 1   2022, for violating Meta’s CSE policy. See Dkt. No. 19, First Amended Complaint (“FAC”) ¶¶ 28,
 2   54. Plaintiff further alleged that he appealed the disablement but a human reviewer from one of the
 3   Vendor Defendants affirmed the disablement after receiving a copy of Plaintiff’s U.S. passport,
 4   which included his photo. FAC ¶¶ 55–56. Plaintiff also alleged that in 2022, “Meta actioned
 5   approximately 105.9 million items under its [CSE] enforcement category[,]” including 92.2 million
 6   on Facebook alone, that 8,100 of those actions were reversed on appeal, and five of the individuals
 7   whose Facebook accounts were restored were white users. FAC ¶¶ 34, 67, 69–73. Based on these
 8   allegations, the FAC summarily asserted that all “Defendants acted because of Plaintiff’s race,”
 9   FAC ¶ 143, and brought claims against each of them under 42 U.S.C. §§ 1981, 1982, 1983, and
10   1985(3). FAC ¶¶ 137–77.
11           Each Defendant moved to dismiss Plaintiff’s operative complaint in the Middle District of
12   Florida, including on the ground that Section 230 barred all of Plaintiff’s claims because they were
13   based on Meta’s alleged disablement of Plaintiff’s Facebook account and a Vendor Defendant’s
14   alleged decision to affirm that disablement. Dkt. Nos. 29, 48, 85, and 96. Meta also moved to
15   transfer the case to this District. Dkt. No. 87. After the court in the Middle District of Florida stayed
16   discovery pending the resolution of Defendants’ motions to dismiss, Plaintiff cross-moved to
17   transfer the case back to the Northern District of California.2 Dkt. No. 108. The case was transferred
18   to this Court. Dkt. No. 121.
19           Following transfer, Plaintiff filed a Motion for Leave to File his SAC, which Defendants
20   did not oppose, noting that the SAC remained deficient for the reasons identified in prior Motions
21   to Dismiss but that Defendants were willing to re-brief their Motions to address Ninth Circuit law.
22   Dkt. Nos. 141, 147. The Court granted Plaintiff’s Motion for Leave to Amend and ordered
23   Defendants to file a consolidated Motion to Dismiss, staying discovery pending resolution of that
24   Motion to Dismiss. See Dkt. No. 151.3
25   2
       While in Florida federal court, Plaintiff also filed a petition for a writ of mandamus with the
     Eleventh Circuit, claiming his case was being mishandled by the district judge and magistrate judge.
26   Dkt. No. 91. The Eleventh Circuit denied that petition. Dkt. No. 109.
     3
       Beyond the claims raised in this action, Plaintiff has also filed several different actions in other
27
     courts raising baseless claims against some combination of the Defendants. These actions include:
28   (1) a defamation action against Meta and counsel for Accenture based on arguments in Accenture’s

 1          The SAC’s Allegations: As before, Plaintiff alleges that he is a “Black citizen of the United
 2   States” who “operated a mobile recreational-vehicle repair business in Florida and adjacent states”
 3   and sourced customers through Facebook. SAC ¶ 24. In particular, the SAC alleges that Plaintiff
 4   “performed third-party contracts with customers and with the National RV Training Academy
 5   through a Facebook account,” Id. ¶ 1, and used his Facebook account to access the “National RV
 6   Training Academy Alumni Group” and to “source[] one hundred percent of his customer and
 7   leads.” Id. ¶¶ 39; 41; see also FAC ¶ 53 (alleging that “[i]n June 2022, Plaintiff began marketing
 8   his RV repair business on Facebook”).
 9          The SAC, however, omits all references to Meta allegedly disabling Plaintiff’s Facebook
10   account pursuant to its CSE policy on July 4, 2022, and instead alleges that “[o]n July 4, 2022,
11   Meta authored a [N]otice” and “used the Notice as the basis for interrupting Plaintiff’s ability to
12   perform third-party contracts through [his Facebook] Account and cutting off Plaintiff’s access to
13   account-resident business property.” SAC ¶ 44. The SAC provides no details regarding what the
14   Notice stated or what content Plaintiff posted to Facebook. The SAC goes on to allege that Plaintiff
15   “appealed the Notice and submitted his United States passport” as “government-issued
16   identification.” Id. ¶¶ 46; 48. The SAC further alleges that one of the Vendor Defendants (without
17   specifying which4) “decided Plaintiff’s appeal adversely to Plaintiff” after receiving his appeal
18   materials including his “profile photograph and … passport.” Id. ¶¶ 49–50. The SAC alleges that
19   “Meta accepted and implemented the [Vendor Defendant’s] adverse appeal decision.” Id. ¶ 51.
20

     Motion to Dismiss in Plaintiff’s original N.D. Cal. Action (Ballentine v. Accenture LLP, et al., No.
22   5:26-cv-472 (M.D. Fla.)), which the district court dismissed based on Plaintiff’s “failure to comply
23   with the Standing Order” regarding the disclosure of the use of artificial intelligence and Plaintiff’s
     “inability to certify compliance with Rule 11 of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure,” Order,
24   Ballentine v. Accenture LLP, et al., No. 5:26-cv-472 (M.D. Fla. July 24, 2026), Dkt. No. 80; (2) a
     Florida state court action raising both the civil rights claims raised in this action and Plaintiff’s
25   defamation claims (Ballentine v. Meta Platforms, Inc., et al., No. 5:26-cv-213 (M.D. Fla.), removed
     from No. 35-2026-CA-000494 (Cir. Ct. Lake Cnty.)); and (3) most recently, a complaint against
26   the National Center for Missing & Exploited Children (“NCMEC”) and its corporate counsel in the
27   Eastern District of Virginia based on allegedly defamatory language in a letter sent by NCMEC to
     Plaintiff in response to a subpoena (Ballentine v. Katie Hall, et al., No. 1:26-cv-2331 (E.D. Va.)).

 1           The SAC also continues to allege that the same five purportedly white comparators named
 2   in the FAC (Steven Ertelt, COMP-1, Abby Covington, @slut.social, and Betty Tompkins, FAC ¶¶
 3   69–73) were treated differently. Again, however, the SAC omits all reference to CSE policy
 4   disablements and instead alleges that Meta “has returned white Facebook account-holders to third-

15   III.    LEGAL STANDARD
16           To survive a motion to dismiss under Rule 12(b)(6), a complaint must include “sufficient
17   factual matter, accepted as true, to ‘state a claim to relief that is plausible on its face.’” Nayab v.
18   Cap. One Bank (USA), N.A., 942 F.3d 480, 495–96 (9th Cir. 2019) (quoting Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556
19   U.S. 662, 678 (2009)). “The plausibility standard … asks for more than a sheer possibility that a
20   defendant has acted unlawfully.” Id. at 496. Although well-pleaded factual allegations are assumed
21   to be true, “the court is not required to accept as true allegations that are merely conclusory,
22   unwarranted deductions of fact, or unreasonable inferences.” Khoja v. Orexigen Therapeutics, Inc.,
23   899 F.3d 988, 1008 (9th Cir. 2018) (citation modified). And while pro se pleadings are construed
24   “liberally,” a pro se plaintiff must still allege “factual matter” sufficient “to state a claim to relief
25   that is plausible on its face.” Johnson v. Lucent Techs., Inc., 653 F.3d 1000, 1010–11 (9th Cir.
26   2011) (citation omitted). Where an amended complaint “omits previously-pled material information
27   that harms Plaintiff’s case,” the Court may consider the prior pleadings because the allegations are
28   “appropriately characterized as judicial admissions.” Jackson v. Loews Hotels, Inc., No. ED CV

18          Plaintiff’s SAC fails because it is barred in its entirety by Section 230(c)(1) of the
19   Communications Decency Act (“CDA”), 47 U.S.C. § 230. Section 230(c)(1) states that “[n]o
20   provider or user of an interactive computer service shall be treated as the publisher or speaker of
21   any information provided by another information content provider.” 47 U.S.C. § 230(c)(1). Section
22   230(e)(3) further states that “[n]o cause of action may be brought and no liability may be imposed
23   under any State or local law that is inconsistent with this section.” 47 U.S.C. § 230(e)(3). The Ninth
24   Circuit has accordingly held that, under Section 230(c)(1), an interactive computer service provider
25   or user cannot be held liable for removing content published on its services by a third party. See
26   Fair Hous. Council of San Fernando Valley v. Roommates.com, LLC, 521 F.3d 1157, 1170–71 (9th
27   Cir. 2008) (“[A]ny activity that can be boiled down to deciding whether to exclude material that
28   third parties seek to post online is perforce immune under section 230.”). And where it is apparent

 5   suspicion, unequal treatment and humiliation”).
 6          D.      Plaintiff’s Allegations Improperly Group the Vendor Defendants Together
 7          Finally, the SAC fails as to each of the Vendor Defendants because it improperly asserts
 8   claims against the Vendor Defendants collectively, without specifying which of the Vendor
 9   Defendants were responsible for the specific acts alleged in the SAC. See TEEC Angel Mgmt, LLC
10   v. Tsingyuan Ventures LLC, No. 24-cv-08991, 2026 WL 1660035, at *1–2 (N.D. Cal. Feb. 27 2026)
11   (dismissing complaint based on finding that “Plaintiffs engage[d] in improper group pleading”
12   where plaintiff referred to defendants “collectively without attributing conduct to any particular
13   Defendant” or otherwise “distinguishing what each entity did”); Beluca Ventures LLC v.
14   Aktiebolag, 622 F. Supp. 3d 806, 816 (N.D. Cal. 2022) (holding that “the Complaint improperly
15   engages in undifferentiated pleading that fails to make clear what allegations are being made
16   against” each defendant where “[a]lmost all of the allegations in the Complaint are made against”
17   one entity, defined to include all the defendants). Here, although the SAC asserts the Section 1981
18   claim against all the Vendor Defendants, it fails to clearly specify which Vendor Defendant that
19   Plaintiff alleges reviewed his Facebook account, or whether Plaintiff is merely guessing that one
20   of the Vendor Defendants reviewed the Facebook account. See SAC ¶¶ 84, 86 (alleging that a
21   “Codefendant,” defined to include Accenture, Genpact and TaskUs, “decided Plaintiff’s appeal”
22   and “but for Plaintiff’s race, the Codefendant would not have decided Plaintiff’s appeal adversely”);
23   see also Beatport LLC v. SoundCloud, Ltd., No. CV 19-847, 2020 WL 3977602, at *5 (C.D. Cal.
24   July 13, 2020) (“It is a basic pleading defect for a complaint to ‘lump’ parties together and to fail
25   to distinguish between named defendants.” (citation omitted)). Accordingly, Plaintiff’s Section
26   1981 claim against the Vendor Defendants is independently subject to dismissal for failure to allege
27   specific conduct as to each Vendor Defendant.
